title: NURS 1017 Unit 6 Case Study 5

question.stem: The nurse reviews the client's history and assessment. Which of the following findings would be consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ptosis that worsens after 60 seconds of looking upward
Blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg
Drooping eyelids and double vision that worsen as the day goes on
Drinks 3 cups of coffee a day
Voice becomes soft and nasal during long conversations
Heart rate 76 beats/min
Arm weakness while blow-drying her hair that recovers after a short rest
Low back pain after gardening
Jaw tires while chewing, so she rests partway through meals

question.explanation:
Hallmark: fatigable weakness. In myasthenia gravis (MG), voluntary muscles weaken with repeated use and recover with rest. Weakness is therefore least in the morning and worst later in the day or after sustained activity.

Ocular muscles are affected first in most clients (ptosis, diplopia). Sustained upward gaze tires the eyelid muscle and brings out the ptosis.

Bulbar muscles (chewing, swallowing, speaking) are often affected: a tiring jaw, a soft nasal voice, choking. Bulbar weakness matters because it threatens the airway.

Proximal limb muscles tire with repeated or sustained use, such as holding the arms up.

Not consistent: back pain after gardening is a common strain, her coffee intake is moderate, and her heart rate and blood pressure are normal.

Also note what she denies: MG affects only the neuromuscular junction, so sensation is normal (numbness and tingling would suggest a nerve problem) and there is no twitching (fasciculations suggest a motor neuron disease such as ALS). Weakness that is worst on waking would be the opposite of the MG pattern.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: In myasthenia gravis, [[drop0]]. With repeated use, the muscle weakens because [[drop1]]. The ice pack improved the ptosis because cold [[drop2]]. The thymus is examined because it [[drop3]].

options.text: the muscle fibers lack the protein dystrophin
the motor neurons in the spinal cord degenerate
the myelin around peripheral nerves is destroyed
antibodies block and destroy acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
lactic acid builds up and damages the muscle fibers
each nerve impulse releases less acetylcholine, and too few receptors remain to respond
the nerve stops conducting impulses altogether
reduces swelling of the eyelid
slows the breakdown of acetylcholine, so more of it reaches the receptors
destroys the antibodies in the eyelid
is often abnormal in myasthenia gravis and is thought to help produce the antibodies
is where the muscle weakness begins
produces acetylcholine for the muscles

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Diagnostic Results and the Nurses' Notes from Day 14 1000.
question.explanation:
Autoimmune mechanism: MG is an antibody-mediated autoimmune disease. Antibodies against the acetylcholine (ACh) receptor on the muscle side of the neuromuscular junction block the receptors, speed their destruction, and activate complement, which damages the folds of the muscle membrane. Fewer receptors mean a weaker signal to contract. (Motor neuron degeneration is ALS; demyelination of peripheral nerves is Guillain-Barré syndrome; absent dystrophin is Duchenne muscular dystrophy.)

Fatigability: with each repeated nerve impulse, the amount of ACh released normally falls a little. In healthy muscle there are plenty of receptors, so this does not matter; in MG there are too few, so contraction fades. This is also what repetitive nerve stimulation shows: a decreasing response.

Ice pack test: cooling slows acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that breaks down ACh, so more ACh is available at the receptors and the eyelid lifts. Heat has the opposite effect, which is why hot weather and hot baths worsen MG.

Thymus: most clients with ACh receptor antibodies have an abnormal thymus (hyperplasia, or a thymoma in about 10% to 15%). The thymus is thought to help start and maintain the autoimmune response.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The client is most likely experiencing [[drop0]], triggered by [[drop1]]. The finding that best shows how serious her condition is, is [[drop2]]. The nurse's priority concern is [[drop3]].

options.text: an anxiety attack
myasthenic crisis
a stroke
cholinergic crisis
the pneumonia and the missed pyridostigmine doses
her anxiety
the low-flow oxygen
the temperature of 38.0° C
the heart rate of 112 beats/min
the SpO₂ of 93%

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 240 1900 and Day 241 0600 and 0610, and the Vital Signs from Day 240 and Day 241.
question.explanation:
Myasthenic crisis is a sudden worsening of MG in which the breathing and bulbar muscles become too weak to maintain ventilation and protect the airway. Common triggers are infection (here, pneumonia with fever), missed or too little cholinesterase inhibitor, surgery, stress, and some medicines.

Why not cholinergic crisis: too much cholinesterase inhibitor can also cause weakness, but with signs of excess acetylcholine (diarrhea, cramping, sweating, excessive secretions, small pupils, slow heart rate). She has missed doses and has none of these signs except pooled saliva, which here comes from being unable to swallow. The provider confirms which crisis it is.

Vital capacity measures the strength of the breathing muscles directly and falls before oxygen saturation does. A vital capacity below about 20 mL/kg (about 1.2 L for a 60-kg client) or a negative inspiratory force weaker than −20 to −30 cm H₂O signals impending respiratory failure. Pulse oximetry stays reassuring until late because the oxygen she is receiving masks hypoventilation.

Priority: airway and breathing. Weak respiratory muscles plus weak swallowing and coughing (aspiration risk) can lead to respiratory arrest within hours.

leftContent.intro: The nurse in a neurology clinic is caring for a 34-year-old female client with drooping eyelids and weakness.

question.stem: Which actions should the nurse take at this time? Select all that apply.

options.text: Measure vital capacity and negative inspiratory force as prescribed and report any further decrease
Rely on pulse oximetry to detect any further decline in breathing
Give thin liquids through a straw to keep her hydrated
Raise the head of the bed and keep suction equipment at the bedside
Encourage the client to walk in the hallway to clear lung secretions
Lay the client flat to rest her breathing muscles
Hold all food, fluids, and oral medications until her swallowing is assessed
Notify the provider and the rapid response team of the falling vital capacity
Stay with the client and reassure her while help is on the way

question.explanation:
Correct: a vital capacity this low means she may soon need ventilatory support, so the provider and the rapid response team are called now. Head elevation helps breathing and reduces aspiration, and suction must be ready because she cannot clear her secretions. Nothing is given by mouth while bulbar weakness makes swallowing unsafe; the nurse tells the provider that oral medicines are being held so other routes can be ordered. Serial vital capacity and negative inspiratory force track her breathing muscle strength. Staying with her reduces anxiety and allows rapid response to deterioration.

Incorrect: exertion worsens fatigable weakness and increases oxygen demand. Thin liquids are the hardest to swallow safely and are easily aspirated. Lying flat makes breathing harder and increases aspiration risk. Pulse oximetry detects respiratory failure late, especially when the client is receiving oxygen; vital capacity and the client's work of breathing are better guides.

question.stem: For each instruction, click to specify whether it is appropriate or not appropriate to include in the client's discharge teaching.

rows.text: Take pyridostigmine on time, about 30 to 60 minutes before meals
Take hot baths to relax your muscles in the evening
Plan demanding tasks for times of the day when you feel strongest, and rest between activities
Skip a dose of pyridostigmine on days when you feel strong
Check with your provider or pharmacist before taking any new medicine, including antibiotics
Wear a medical alert bracelet that says you have myasthenia gravis
Eat your largest meal in the evening, when you are hungriest
Seek emergency care for trouble swallowing, a weak cough, or shortness of breath

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 255 1000 and the Vital Signs from Day 255.
question.explanation:
Appropriate: pyridostigmine (a cholinesterase inhibitor) works for 3 to 4 hours, so doses are taken on time, and before meals so chewing and swallowing are strongest while eating. Energy conservation (doing demanding tasks when strength is best, resting between activities) works with the fatigable pattern. Many medicines can worsen MG (for example some antibiotics such as fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides, magnesium, and beta-blockers), so new medicines are checked first. A medical alert bracelet informs emergency staff. Difficulty swallowing, a weak cough or breathlessness can signal a crisis and need emergency care.

Not appropriate: heat worsens neuromuscular transmission (hot baths, saunas, hot weather). Missing doses can trigger a crisis, as it did before. Fatigue is worst in the evening, so large evening meals raise the risk of choking; smaller meals at times of best strength are safer.

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it indicates that the plan of care has been effective or not effective.

rows.text: “I sometimes skip my bedtime dose when I feel strong.”
Ptosis only late in the evening; double vision rare
Choking on liquids at supper, with a weak voice by bedtime
“I started a hot yoga class to build up my strength.”
“I got my flu shot, and I stay away from people with colds.”

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 285 1000 and 1015 and the Vital Signs from Day 285.
question.explanation:
Effective: her vital capacity has recovered to a safe level, her ocular symptoms are mild and limited to the end of the day (expected in MG), and she has taken steps that reduce the risk of another crisis (medical alert bracelet, influenza vaccination with an inactivated vaccine, avoiding infection).

Not effective: skipping doses and choking with a weak voice in the evening show that bulbar weakness is not controlled at the end of the day; this puts her at risk of aspiration and another crisis. The nurse reinforces taking every dose on time and reports the evening choking to the provider. Hot yoga exposes her to heat, which worsens neuromuscular transmission; gentle exercise in a cool environment, paced with rest, is safer.
